new_statements.quote: 声調 (T) は, I. 低平・長 ([22~21]), II. 高降・長 ([442]), III. 高降または高平・短・緩い緊喉 (['42~'44]), IV. 低平・短・堅い緊喉 [ʔ22] の四つと軽声があり, ピッチの高低と緊喉・非緊喉の音声特徴をもとに整理すれば次のようになる。 [...] 第三声と第四声の声調型が, ラングーン=マンダレー方言の場合と逆になっていることが注目される。 [...] 軽声は母音記号 /ə/ で示す。 (p. 159) — /ə/ は軽声化音節にのみ現われる。 (p. 158)
new_statements.translation: The tones (T) are four — I. low level, long ([22~21]); II. high falling, long ([442]); III. high falling or high level, short, with lax glottal constriction (['42~'44]); IV. low level, short, with tight glottal constriction ([ʔ22]) — plus a light (reduced/neutral) tone; arranged by pitch height and constricted vs. non-constricted phonation they come out as follows [table]. [...] It is notable that the tone shapes of the third and fourth tones are the reverse of those in the Rangoon-Mandalay dialect. [...] The light tone is shown by the vowel symbol /ə/. (p. 159) — /ə/ appears only in light-toned syllables. (p. 158)

new_statements.rule_in_words: Taungyo is described as a tone language of Burmese type: four lexical tones (low-level long; high-falling long; high-falling/high-level short creaky; low-level short glottalized) distinguished by pitch and glottal constriction, plus an atonic 'light-tone' (軽声) syllable type whose only vowel is /ə/ (the Burmese-style reduced minor syllable, e.g. /ʔəwæʔ/ 'leaf', /pəkanplâ/ 'plate'). The source makes no statement about word stress or accent; the only prominence-related notion is the tonal vs. reduced (light-tone) syllable contrast.
new_statements.exceptions: None on stress. On tone: the Nanman ('big Taungyo') sub-dialect of the third informant is stated to have the same tone pattern ('声調の型は同じである', p. 159); the second informant lacks syllabic /ɴ/. Tone notation: unmarked = tone I, circumflex = II, acute = III, -(ʔ) = IV.
new_statements.domain_note: Citation forms / wordlist items (Hattori basic vocabulary list and ILCAA questionnaire) elicited from speakers of Heho-Myegya village near Taunggyi (1978-79) and Naungmu village, Pinlaung (1972); syllable-level tone description, no phrase-level prosody.
new_statements.identity_note: Yabu 1981 describes what he calls the 'small Taungyo' sub-dialect (/tɔnrɤ̂ ɲæ/, first and second informants from Heho-Myegya village, Nyaungshwe Township, near Taunggyi) and, more briefly, the 'Nanman' or 'big Taungyo' sub-dialect (/nɔʔmɔn tɔnrɤ̂/, third informant from Naungmu village, Pinlaung Township), stating that the tone pattern is the same in both. Both fall under Glottolog taun1248 (Taungyo), which Glottolog and Yabu treat as a dialect of Burmese (Burmish); no separate glottocodes for the sub-dialects.

sources.note: Section 3 (phoneme system, pp. 157-159) gives consonants, vowels and four tones plus a 'light tone' (軽声) reduced-syllable class marked by /ə/ (p. 158: /ə/ occurs only in light-toned syllables; p. 159: tone inventory, tones III/IV reversed relative to Rangoon-Mandalay Burmese; Nanman sub-dialect has the same tone pattern). No mention of word stress or accent (強勢/アクセント) anywhere in the phonology section; the rest of the paper is a wordlist and conversation text.

sources.citation: Taylor, L. F. 1921/1922. The dialects of Burmese (I). Journal of the Burma Research Society 11(2): 89-97 + 4 tables. (Studies in Indo-Chinese Philology No. 1.)
sources.note: Comparative survey of nine Burmese dialects incl. Taungyo ('another primitive form of Burmese... spoken in the west of the Southern Shan States', p. 92); Burmese described as 'tonal and monosyllabic'. The comparative-vocabulary table key labels syllable types 1-4 as 'high, stopped unstressed', 'ordinary long unmarked', 'long stressed', 'high, checked stressed' — a 1920s tone notation applied to all dialects, not a word-stress statement for Taungyo.
